gap: No result ChatGPT got (of the three under-$300 guides I opened) states that the "1,500 W lifting" / X-Boost figure is reached by lowering the outlet voltage while the inverter's rated watts stay the same, or that the mode is unavailable while the station is charging from the wall.
standout_why: I compared against Nineteen Lab (the cited page), Portable Power Rank and Power Station Picks; I did not open the other results (deal roundups and price trackers). Nineteen Lab already says Power Lifting is "for resistive loads only: heaters and kettles, never a compressor", gives the Elite 30 V2's 4.5 W standby and the Wh × 0.85 ÷ W runtime formula. Power Station Picks says Power Lifting "runs resistive loads up to 1,500W". Portable Power Rank calls 1,500 W a "peak" and does not explain it. None gives the voltage-reduction mechanism in the maker's words, the no-AC-charging condition, or the default on/off state. So rivals have the headline (resistive only) and lack the why and the charging condition. I could not source the finding I expected to be stronger, the ECO-mode auto shut-off at low loads, which none of the three pages mentions.
decides: It confirms the ranking rather than changing it. Rank on continuous AC watts (600 W BLUETTI Elite 30 V2, 300 W Elite 30 mini, 200 W Tenergy T320, and the rivals' rated figures), never on lifting or X-Boost numbers. A kettle or heater on a lifting mode gets a lowered voltage, so it heats slower, and the mode is off the table when the unit sits plugged in as a UPS. It backs ChatGPT's line that none of these suits a space heater, and adds the reason.

findings.value: "intelligent voltage control that marginally reduces voltage, allowing you to power devices with a lower-rated inverter"
findings.note: EcoFlow's own wording. The page lists reference appliances (electric kettle 1,500 W, hair dryer 1,600 W, electric heater 2,200 W) and gives no per-model X-Boost watts, so it does not state the RIVER 2 Max figure.

findings.label: Named tester's result under X-Boost
findings.value: The Solar Lab: a heat gun ran "only at about 70% to 80% efficiency"; "X-Boost does not provide a true power increase."
findings.source_title: EcoFlow X-Boost feature explained (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The article does not name the station, the heat gun's rated watts, or measured volts and watts, and shows no date beyond © 2026. Its 90 V / 1,350 W figures are worked examples, not measurements.

findings.label: Arithmetic: a 1,500 W kettle held to 600 W
findings.value: about 76 V at the element; about 2.5× the boil time
findings.source_title: Bluetti AC60 user manual, page 12 of 44 (ManualsLib copy)
findings.note: My arithmetic, not a maker figure. Element resistance = 120² ÷ 1,500 = 9.6 Ω; at 600 W, V = √(600 × 9.6) ≈ 75.9 V; 1,500 ÷ 600 = 2.5. It assumes the inverter holds its 600 W rating, as the AC60 manual words it. BLUETTI's Elite 30 V2 page instead says "momentarily reach up to 1,500W", so do not print this as an Elite 30 V2 measurement.

findings.label: What the cited page already states on this angle
findings.value: Elite 30 V2: "1,500W Power Lifting for resistive loads only." RIVER 2 Max: "X-Boost pushes the 500W inverter to 1,000W for careful kitchen bursts". "A compressor fridge pulls 700W or more at startup". "Runtime is watt-hours x 0.85 / watts"
findings.source_title: Best Portable Power Stations Under $300 (2026): Honest Tier Picks | Nineteen Lab
findings.note: It lists no prices and does not cover ECO mode, auto shut-off, temperature limits, the voltage mechanism or the no-charging condition. The 1,000 W X-Boost figure for the RIVER 2 Max is Nineteen Lab's; I could not check it on EcoFlow's page.
